body.passage:
A. Every Saturday morning, before the city fully wakes, a quiet stream of people arrives at the Riverside Animal Shelter. They sign in, collect their name badges and head straight for the kennels. Most of them hold ordinary jobs during the week - teachers, accountants, nurses - but here they are known simply as volunteers. For many, the decision to give up free time for abandoned cats and dogs began with a single visit that they could not forget. Shelter managers say that without this unpaid workforce, the facility could barely function; paid staff number only nine, while volunteers exceed eighty.

B. Becoming a volunteer is not as simple as turning up with good intentions. Applicants must complete a written form, attend an orientation session and pass a short training course covering animal handling, hygiene and safety. The training emphasises that even friendly animals can behave unpredictably when frightened. New volunteers are paired with experienced mentors for their first month, and only after this probation period may they work unsupervised. The shelter rejects roughly one applicant in five, usually because of unreliable availability rather than unsuitable character.

C. Daily duties vary enormously. Mornings are devoted to cleaning: kennels must be scrubbed, bedding replaced and food prepared according to each animal's medical plan. Volunteers record every detail, from appetite to unusual behaviour, because a dog that refuses breakfast may be signalling illness. Afternoons shift towards enrichment - the activities that keep animals mentally healthy while they wait for homes. These include puzzle feeders, grooming sessions and supervised play in the yard.

D. Dog walking is the task most volunteers request first, yet it demands more skill than newcomers expect. Shelter dogs often arrive with little training and high energy, so walkers are taught to use consistent commands and to avoid tense leash pulling, which can increase anxiety. The shelter's behaviour coordinator explains that a calm, confident walker teaches a dog more about the outside world than any classroom-style drill. Volunteers who walk the same dog regularly frequently notice progress within weeks: a once-cowering animal may begin to approach strangers or respond to its name.

E. Cats require a different approach altogether. Because felines are highly sensitive to noise and crowding, the cat room follows strict quiet rules, and volunteers sit still, allowing the animals to initiate contact. This process, called socialisation, gradually rebuilds trust in cats that may have spent months on the streets. Some volunteers describe the first time a previously hidden cat climbs onto their lap as the single most rewarding moment of their service.

F. The work is not emotionally easy. Volunteers form attachments to animals that may be ill, elderly or unlikely to be adopted quickly, and occasionally they must face euthanasia decisions made by veterinary staff. The shelter offers monthly support meetings where volunteers can discuss difficult cases, and managers watch carefully for burnout - the exhaustion that follows prolonged emotional strain. Surprisingly, turnover remains low; most volunteers stay for at least two years, and several have served for over a decade.

G. Adoption events are the public face of the shelter's efforts. Twice a month, volunteers transport animals to a shopping centre, set up enclosures and speak to potential adopters. Their role is to match families with suitable pets, which sometimes means gently discouraging an applicant whose lifestyle would not suit a high-energy dog. When a match succeeds, volunteers often keep in touch with adopters, receiving photographs of animals lounging in living rooms they once could only dream of.

H. For those considering volunteering, experienced members offer consistent advice: start with realistic expectations, accept that progress is slow, and never underestimate the value of simply sitting quietly with a frightened animal. As one long-serving volunteer puts it, the shelter does not ask people to save every animal - only to improve the days of the ones in front of them. That modest ambition, repeated week after week, is what keeps the kennel doors open and the animals within them hopeful.

body.passage_title: Behind the Kennel Doors: Life as an Animal Shelter Volunteer

body.passage:
A. Every year, the world discards more than 60 million tonnes of electronic equipment, from smartphones and laptops to refrigerators and medical devices. This stream of discarded technology, known as e-waste, is growing roughly five times faster than documented recycling rates. Only about one fifth of global e-waste is formally collected and recycled; the rest ends up in landfills, incinerators or informal dumps, where toxic substances can leak into soil and groundwater. Researchers warn that if current trends continue, the volume of e-waste could reach 82 million tonnes by 2030, making it the fastest-growing domestic waste stream on the planet.

B. The reason e-waste is so hazardous lies in its composition. A single mobile phone contains dozens of materials, including lead, mercury, cadmium and flame retardants that are harmful to human health and the environment. When devices are crushed in landfills or burned in the open air, these substances are released and can travel long distances. Exposure has been linked to damage to the nervous system, respiratory illness and developmental problems in children. Yet the same devices also contain valuable metals such as gold, silver, copper and palladium. One tonne of circuit boards can contain up to 200 grams of gold, roughly forty times the concentration found in typical gold ore.

C. This combination of danger and value has created a paradox. E-waste is simultaneously one of the most toxic and one of the most resource-rich waste streams in existence. Economists estimate that the raw materials embedded in the world's annual e-waste output are worth over 60 billion dollars, yet most of this value is never recovered. Instead, mining companies continue to extract virgin metals, a process that consumes enormous amounts of energy and water and generates far greater carbon emissions than recycling would.

D. A large share of the world's discarded electronics travels to developing countries, particularly in West Africa and South Asia. At sites such as the Agbogbloshie scrapyard in Ghana, cleared in 2021, workers dismantled imported devices by hand, often without protective equipment, to extract copper wire and other sellable components. Critics describe these sites as dumping grounds for the industrialised world. However, the picture is more complicated than it first appears. Many shipments are legal: functioning second-hand computers and phones are exported to markets where demand for affordable technology is high. The problem arises when devices that are broken or obsolete are mixed in with working ones, a practice that international agreements such as the Basel Convention are supposed to prevent but which enforcement agencies struggle to police.

E. Governments have responded with a patchwork of policies. The European Union's WEEE Directive obliges manufacturers to finance the collection and recycling of the equipment they sell, and several countries have introduced 'right to repair' laws that require companies to make spare parts and repair manuals available to consumers. Japan has gone further than most, running a state-supported system in which consumers pay a small recycling fee when they dispose of certain appliances. Meanwhile, in the United States, regulation varies from state to state, and federal legislation remains limited. Analysts note that where producer responsibility is weak, collection rates tend to be low, because consumers have little incentive to hand in old devices.

F. The recycling industry itself faces technical obstacles. Modern gadgets are deliberately designed to be thin, light and compact, which makes them difficult to disassemble. Batteries glued into casings, screens fused to frames and miniature screws all slow down manual dismantling. Automated shredding plants can process large volumes quickly, but they recover only a fraction of the rare metals inside, and some processes destroy materials that could have been reused intact. Researchers are therefore exploring 'urban mining' technologies, including robotic disassembly and chemical processes that dissolve circuit boards and release metals selectively. Early trials are promising, but the technologies remain expensive and are not yet widely deployed.

G. Consumer behaviour is another crucial piece of the puzzle. Surveys consistently show that people keep old phones in drawers rather than returning them, largely because they are unsure where to take them or worry about the personal data stored on them. Campaigns that offer trade-in discounts, secure data-wiping services and convenient drop-off points have measurably increased collection rates. In one European trial, placing collection bins in supermarkets raised participation by nearly a third within six months, suggesting that convenience matters more than environmental awareness alone.

H. Ultimately, experts argue that recycling alone cannot solve the e-waste problem. The most effective strategy is to slow the flow of electronics in the first place by designing devices that last longer, can be repaired easily and use fewer hazardous materials. Some manufacturers have begun to advertise repairability scores and modular designs, and investors increasingly treat electronic durability as a marker of good corporate practice. If these shifts continue, the e-waste mountain may grow more slowly than feared, though few believe it will stop growing altogether.

body.passage_title: The Global Challenge of Electronic Waste

body.passage:
A. Every third bite of food we eat exists because of an insect most people never notice. Bees, butterflies, hoverflies, beetles and even some species of bat and bird transfer pollen between flowering plants, allowing them to set seed and fruit. Scientists estimate that around 75 percent of the world's leading food crops depend to some degree on animal pollination, and the crops that rely on it — apples, almonds, coffee, cocoa, blueberries and squash, among many others — supply the majority of vitamins, minerals and antioxidants in the human diet. Without pollinators, agriculture would not collapse entirely, since staple grains such as wheat, rice and maize are wind-pollinated, but our plates would be dramatically less colourful, less nutritious and far more expensive.

B. The economic value of this service is staggering. A widely cited global assessment put the annual value of crops directly dependent on pollinators at between 235 and 577 billion dollars. In the United States alone, honeybees trucked across the country to pollinate almond orchards in California generate a service worth more than the honey they produce by a factor of dozens. In China, in parts of Sichuan province where wild bees have vanished, farmers now pollinate pear trees by hand, dabbing pollen onto blossoms with brushes tied to bamboo poles. The practice works, but it is laborious, costly and, according to researchers who have studied it, a warning of what large-scale pollinator loss could force upon agriculture elsewhere.

C. Despite their importance, pollinators are in trouble. Populations of wild bees and butterflies have declined across North America and Europe, and commercial honeybee colonies suffer significant annual losses. The causes are multiple and interact with one another: habitat loss as hedgerows and wildflower meadows are ploughed under, exposure to certain pesticides, parasites such as the varroa mite, and the spread of diseases that move easily between managed hives and wild insects. Climate change adds a further layer of stress, because warming can desynchronise the moment when flowers open from the period when pollinators are active, leaving each waiting for the other.

D. The consequences for farming are already measurable. Growers of pollinator-dependent crops report lower and less stable yields, and fruit is sometimes smaller or misshapen when pollination is incomplete. In regions where wild pollinators have disappeared, farmers face a stark choice: pay for managed hives, hand-pollinate, or switch to less nutritious crops that do not need animal pollination. Each option carries costs — financial, nutritional or both — and the burden falls hardest on smallholders in developing countries, who often cannot afford rented hives and depend on their local environment for the pollination their fields receive.

E. Fortunately, the news is not uniformly grim, and a growing body of research points to practical solutions. Studies across five continents found that farms surrounded by natural habitat enjoyed substantially better pollination than those in intensively farmed monocultures. Even modest changes help: planting strips of wildflowers along field margins, leaving patches of bare ground where ground-nesting bees can burrow, and staggering crops so that flowers are available throughout the season all measurably increase the number and diversity of visiting insects. In one trial in the United Kingdom, adding just a few hectares of wildflower habitat to large farms raised the number of pollinating insects enough to boost yields in adjacent crop rows, allowing the habitat to pay for itself within a few years.

F. Policy is beginning to follow the science. The European Union has restricted several insecticides linked to bee declines, and more than a dozen countries have adopted national pollinator strategies that combine habitat restoration, farmer incentives and monitoring programmes. Some agribusiness firms now rent out not only hives but also 'bee-friendly' field margins, and certification schemes reward growers who set aside land for pollinators. Critics argue that these measures remain voluntary and patchy, and that pesticide regulation in many countries still lags behind the evidence, but the direction of travel is clear: pollinators are increasingly treated as infrastructure, as essential to farming as soil or water.

G. Ultimately, protecting pollinators is less about saving charismatic insects than about securing a foundation of the food system. The most encouraging lesson from recent research is that agriculture and pollinators are not natural enemies. Farms designed with flowering hedgerows, diverse rotations and reduced chemical inputs can support abundant wild bees while remaining profitable, and in several documented cases they out-yield conventional neighbours in pollinator-dependent crops. The invisible workforce asks for little: a place to nest, flowers to feed on, and freedom from poison. Providing these, farmers and consumers alike would be repaid many times over at the checkout and on the plate.

body.passage_title: The Invisible Workforce: Pollinators and the Future of Farming

body.passage:
A. Few natural phenomena have captured human imagination as persistently as the rainbow. Ancient cultures across the world wove it into their myths, seeing it as a bridge between gods and mortals or a sign of promise after storms. Yet long before these stories were written down, careful observers had already begun to ask a more practical question: what exactly is a rainbow, and why does it always appear in the same shape and position relative to the person looking at it? The answer, it turns out, lies in a remarkable interplay of light, water and geometry.

B. The scientific study of the rainbow began in earnest in the seventeenth century. René Descartes famously traced the path of a single ray of sunlight through an idealised spherical raindrop, calculating precisely where the light would exit after being refracted on entry, reflected once inside the drop, and refracted again on leaving. His calculations revealed that light emerging from a raindrop is concentrated along a particular angle, about 42 degrees from the point directly opposite the sun. This 'rainbow angle' explains the most striking feature of the phenomenon: every observer sees their own personal rainbow, formed from a different set of raindrops, and no two people ever see exactly the same arc.

C. Descartes explained the shape and position of the rainbow, but the colours remained a puzzle until Isaac Newton turned his attention to optics. Newton passed sunlight through a glass prism and demonstrated that white light is not a single entity but a mixture of colours, each bending by a slightly different amount as it passes from air into a denser medium. Red light bends least, violet most. Inside a raindrop, this separation happens twice, so the colours emerge spread into a band. The familiar sequence of red, orange, yellow, green, blue and violet is therefore not a property of the raindrop itself but a direct display of the physics of light dispersion.

D. Not all rainbows are created equal, however. The most common type, the primary rainbow, is produced by one internal reflection within each droplet. A secondary rainbow, which appears fainter and higher in the sky, results from two internal reflections. Each extra reflection costs brightness, which is why secondary bows are roughly one-tenth as intense as primary ones. More intriguingly, the extra reflection reverses the order of the colours, so in a secondary rainbow red appears on the inner edge of the arc rather than the outer edge. Between the two bows lies a noticeably darker region, known since antiquity and named Alexander's dark band after the Greek philosopher who first described it.

E. Under unusual conditions, even more exotic bows can appear. When the sun is low and the air below the observer is filled with fine droplets, as when looking down on fog or cloud from a mountain or an aircraft, a small circular bow may be seen surrounding the observer's own shadow: the glory. On rare occasions, observers report a 'supernumerary rainbow' — a series of faint green and purple bands just inside the main arc. These cannot be explained by Descartes' simple ray model, because they arise from interference, the wave property of light in which overlapping waves reinforce or cancel one another. Their existence was one of the earliest clues that light behaves as a wave, a fact that would transform physics in the nineteenth century.

F. Modern science has extended the study of rainbows far beyond visible light. Physicists now calculate rainbow phenomena for radio waves, X-rays and even atomic particles, and the same mathematics describes phenomena in quantum scattering. Meanwhile, atmospheric scientists exploit the rainbow's sensitivity to droplet size: the sharpness and width of a bow reveal information about the rain that produces it. There is also a cultural dimension to the research. Surveys of historical records show that descriptions of rainbows vary between eras and languages, with some traditions naming fewer colours than the six or seven familiar to modern readers. Newton himself originally listed five colours before adding orange and indigo, apparently to make the number match a musical scale. The rainbow, it seems, is as much a product of the human eye and mind as of sunlight and rain — a reminder that even the simplest wonders of nature reward a second, more careful look.

explanation.explanation_vi: Đoạn D nêu rằng mỗi lần phản chiếu thêm làm giảm độ sáng, khiến cung phụ chỉ bằng khoảng một phần mười cung chính.

questions.prompt: In which paragraph is the following information found? A reference to a discovery that challenged a purely ray-based explanation of rainbows.

explanation.explanation_en: Paragraph E explains that supernumerary bows arise from interference and were early evidence that light behaves as a wave.
explanation.explanation_vi: Đoạn E giải thích rằng cung thừa phát sinh từ giao thoa và là bằng chứng sớm cho thấy ánh sáng có tính chất sóng.

questions.prompt: In which paragraph is the following information found? An account of how the number of rainbow colours was influenced by non-scientific considerations.

explanation.explanation_en: Paragraph F mentions Newton adding orange and indigo to match a musical scale, a non-scientific reason.
explanation.explanation_vi: Đoạn F nói rằng Newton thêm màu cam và indigo để khớp với thang âm nhạc, một lý do không thuộc khoa học.

questions.prompt: In which paragraph is the following information found? A description of an experiment proving that white light is composed of several colours.

explanation.explanation_en: Paragraph C describes Newton's prism experiment showing white light is a mixture of colours.
explanation.explanation_vi: Đoạn C mô tả thí nghiệm lăng kính của Newton chứng minh ánh sáng trắng là hỗn hợp nhiều màu.

questions.prompt: Careful observers were asking about rainbows before the myths about them were written down.

explanation.explanation_en: Paragraph A says that long before these stories were written down, careful observers had already begun to ask what a rainbow is.
explanation.explanation_vi: Đoạn A nói rằng từ lâu trước khi những câu chuyện này được ghi lại, những người quan sát cẩn thận đã bắt đầu đặt câu hỏi cầu vồng là gì.

questions.prompt: Descartes' calculations showed that two observers standing side by side see exactly the same rainbow.

explanation.explanation_en: Paragraph B states that each observer sees a personal rainbow formed from different raindrops, so no two people see the same arc.
explanation.explanation_vi: Đoạn B khẳng định mỗi người thấy cầu vồng riêng từ các giọt mưa khác nhau, nên không ai thấy cùng một cung.

questions.prompt: Newton discovered that violet light bends more than red light inside a raindrop.

explanation.explanation_en: Paragraph C states red bends least and violet most as light passes into a denser medium.
explanation.explanation_vi: Đoạn C nêu rõ ánh sáng đỏ khúc xạ ít nhất và tím nhiều nhất khi đi vào môi trường đặc hơn.

questions.prompt: Alexander's dark band is caused by water droplets absorbing light between the two bows.

explanation.explanation_en: Paragraph D names the dark band but gives no cause for it, so the reason is not stated.
explanation.explanation_vi: Đoạn D chỉ nêu tên dải tối nhưng không cho biết nguyên nhân hình thành nó.

questions.prompt: Complete the sentence with NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage. Descartes calculated that light from a raindrop is concentrated at an angle of about 42 degrees from the point directly opposite the ______.

explanation.explanation_en: Paragraph B states the angle is measured from the point directly opposite the sun.
explanation.explanation_vi: Đoạn B nêu góc 42 độ được tính từ điểm đối diện trực tiếp với mặt trời.

questions.prompt: Complete the sentence with NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage. In a secondary rainbow, the colour red appears on the ______ of the arc.

explanation.explanation_en: Paragraph D says the extra reflection reverses the colour order, placing red on the inner edge.
explanation.explanation_vi: Đoạn D cho biết phản chiếu thêm đảo ngược thứ tự màu, khiến đỏ nằm ở mép trong của cung.

questions.prompt: Complete the sentence with NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage. A glory appears as a small circular bow around the observer's own ______.

explanation.explanation_en: Paragraph E says a small circular bow may be seen surrounding the observer's own shadow: the glory.
explanation.explanation_vi: Đoạn E nói có thể thấy một vòng cung tròn nhỏ bao quanh bóng của chính người quan sát: đó là hiện tượng glory.

questions.prompt: Complete the sentence with NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage. Supernumerary rainbows are produced by the wave property of light known as ______.

explanation.explanation_en: Paragraph E states supernumerary bows arise from interference between overlapping light waves.
explanation.explanation_vi: Đoạn E khẳng định cung thừa phát sinh từ giao thoa giữa các sóng ánh sáng chồng lên nhau.

questions.prompt: Complete the sentence with NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage. The sharpness and width of a rainbow give scientists information about the ______ that produces it.

explanation.explanation_en: Paragraph F says the bow's characteristics reveal information about the rain producing it.
explanation.explanation_vi: Đoạn F nói rằng đặc điểm của cầu vồng cung cấp thông tin về cơn mưa tạo ra nó.

questions.prompt: Complete the sentence with NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage. Newton originally listed five colours before adding two more to match a ______.

explanation.explanation_en: Paragraph F states Newton added orange and indigo so the number of colours would match a musical scale.
explanation.explanation_vi: Đoạn F cho biết Newton thêm hai màu để số màu khớp với một thang âm nhạc.

_provenance.cefr_reasoning: The passage is a complex academic text on a concrete scientific topic with abstract elements, featuring technical vocabulary (refraction, dispersion, interference, quantum scattering), passive constructions, and dense informational paragraphs. Question types (paragraph matching, True/False/Not Given, two-word completion) and the need to distinguish stated vs. unstated information align with B2 reading demands. Some vocabulary and inference depth approach C1, but overall the text and tasks fit B2 well.

body.prompt: Part 1: Introduction and interview. The examiner will ask you some questions about yourself and about deserts and the environment. Answer the following questions in turn: 1) Where do you live, and what is the landscape like there? 2) Have you ever visited a desert or a very dry region? What was it like? 3) Do you prefer hot, dry weather or cool, rainy weather? Why? 4) Would you like to travel through a desert one day? Why or why not? 5) What do you usually do to stay cool on a very hot day?

_provenance.cefr_reasoning: The task requires discussing abstract environmental topics (desertification, causes, solutions), giving opinions with justification, and using topic-specific vocabulary like overgrazing, deforestation, and water management. While the interview format is accessible, the content demands extended discourse on concrete and abstract topics with reasons and examples, matching B2 speaking descriptors.

explanation.text: This is an interview-style task. Give short, direct answers of two to four sentences each. Extend your answers with reasons and examples, especially when discussing desertification, its causes such as overgrazing and deforestation, and possible solutions like tree planting and better water management.
explanation.text_vi: Đây là dạng bài phỏng vấn. Trả lời ngắn gọn, trực tiếp, mỗi câu từ hai đến bốn câu. Mở rộng câu trả lời bằng lý do và ví dụ, đặc biệt khi nói về sự sa mạc hóa, nguyên nhân như chăn thả quá mức và phá rừng, cùng các giải pháp như trồng cây và quản lý nguồn nước tốt hơn.

body.prompt:
Part 1: Introduction and interview. The examiner will ask you several short questions about yourself and the topic of rainbows. Answer each question naturally in two to four sentences.

1. Do you remember seeing a rainbow when you were a child? What was it like?
2. How do you feel when you see a rainbow in the sky?
3. Have you ever learned why rainbows appear? What do you know about the science behind them?
4. Do you think rainbows look the same to everyone who sees them? Why or why not?
5. Are there any stories or beliefs about rainbows in your country?
6. If you could see a rainbow every day, would you still find it special?

_provenance.cefr_reasoning: The task requires extended personal responses on a concrete topic with abstract speculation (e.g., whether rainbows look the same to everyone), plus B2-level vocabulary such as 'refraction', 'atmospheric conditions', and 'superstition'. The interview format with justification and hypothetical conditionals aligns with B2 speaking descriptors.

explanation.text: Answer each question directly, then extend with a reason, example, or personal memory. Use B2-level language such as 'vivid', 'atmospheric conditions', 'refraction', and 'superstition', and keep your answers natural rather than memorised.
explanation.text_vi: Trả lời trực tiếp từng câu hỏi, sau đó mở rộng bằng lý do, ví dụ hoặc kỷ niệm cá nhân. Sử dụng từ vựng trình độ B2 như 'vivid', 'atmospheric conditions', 'refraction', 'superstition' và trả lời tự nhiên, không thuộc lòng.

body.prompt:
In this first part of the Speaking test, the examiner will ask you some general questions about yourself and the topic of the telephone. Answer each question in two or three sentences.

1. How often do you use your phone during a typical day?
2. Do you prefer talking on the phone or texting? Why?
3. Can you describe how your family used the telephone when you were younger?
4. Do you think the invention of the telephone changed people's lives more than the internet has? Why or why not?
5. Would you like to live without a phone for a week? What would be the hardest part?

_provenance.cefr_reasoning: The questions cover familiar, everyday topics (phone use, texting, family habits) requiring simple past and present tenses, opinions with reasons, and basic hypotheticals ('Would you like...'). While the final question invites some comparison and speculation, the vocabulary and structures remain within B1 range; the task does not demand the abstract argumentation or complex language typical of B2.

explanation.text: Give full, natural answers of two or three sentences for each question. Extend your responses with reasons and examples, use a range of past and present tenses, and speak fluently without long pauses.
explanation.text_vi: Trả lời đầy đủ và tự nhiên từ hai đến ba câu cho mỗi câu hỏi. Mở rộng câu trả lời bằng lý do và ví dụ, sử dụng đa dạng các thì quá khứ và hiện tại, và nói trôi chảy không ngập ngừng.

body.prompt:
Part 1: Introduction and interview. Answer the following questions about delivery services and transport in your daily life.

1. Do you often order things online and have them delivered to your home? What kinds of things do you usually order?
2. How do delivery drivers usually bring parcels to your area — by van, motorbike, or on foot? Do you think this works well?
3. Have you noticed more electric vehicles in your city recently, such as electric vans or buses? What do you think of them?
4. Would you prefer to work as a delivery driver for a company that uses electric vans? Why or why not?

_provenance.cefr_reasoning: The task is an IELTS Speaking Part 1 style interview with familiar, everyday topics (online shopping, deliveries, electric vehicles). Questions use simple present, present perfect, and basic modals ('would you prefer'), with common vocabulary and no complex syntax or abstract discussion. Producing short developed answers with reasons and examples is a B1-level speaking demand, below the B2 target.

explanation.text: This is an IELTS Speaking Part 1 style interview. Give short but developed answers of two to four sentences each. Extend your responses with reasons and examples, for example describing what you order online, how deliveries reach your neighbourhood, your impressions of electric vehicles, and your opinion about working as a delivery driver. Speak naturally and avoid memorised answers.
explanation.text_vi: Đây là phần phỏng vấn theo phong cách IELTS Speaking Part 1. Hãy trả lời ngắn gọn nhưng có triển khai, mỗi câu từ hai đến bốn câu. Mở rộng câu trả lời bằng lý do và ví dụ, ví dụ mô tả những gì bạn thường mua online, cách hàng hóa được giao đến khu vực của bạn, ấn tượng của bạn về xe điện, và quan điểm về việc làm tài xế giao hàng. Nói tự nhiên và tránh trả lời thuộc lòng.

body.prompt: Part 1: Introduction and interview. Answer the following questions about weekends and camping. 1) Do you usually spend your weekends at home or going out? Why? 2) Have you ever been on a camping trip? What was it like? 3) What do you think people enjoy most about camping? 4) Would you prefer camping in a forest or near a beach? Why?

_provenance.cefr_reasoning: The task asks for personal opinions and experiences using present perfect, past tenses, and preference structures on familiar everyday topics (weekends, camping). While the target is B2, the required language (present perfect, simple preferences, reasons and examples) and concrete, familiar topics align with B1 rather than B2's complex/abstract discourse demands.

explanation.text: Give full, natural answers of two to four sentences each. Extend your responses with reasons and examples rather than replying with a single word, and use past tenses and preferences language where appropriate.
explanation.text_vi: Trả lời đầy đủ, tự nhiên, mỗi câu từ hai đến bốn câu. Mở rộng câu trả lời bằng lý do và ví dụ thay vì trả lời ngắn gọn, và sử dụng thì quá khứ cùng cấu trúc diễn đạt sở thích khi phù hợp.

body.prompt: Let's talk about team sports. Do you play or follow any team sports? What do you think people gain from playing in a team rather than alone? Can you describe a time when being part of a team helped you or someone you know?

_provenance.cefr_reasoning: The task requires extended discourse (5 minutes) on a semi-abstract topic (benefits of teamwork vs. individual activity), narrating a past experience, and explaining abstract concepts like cooperation and shared responsibility. This demands organized, extended speech with justification and examples, consistent with B2 speaking descriptors, though the vocabulary itself is accessible.

explanation.text: Answer each question in turn with two to four sentences. Give personal examples, explain the benefits of teamwork such as cooperation, communication and shared responsibility, and speak naturally for the full time.
explanation.text_vi: Trả lời lần lượt từng câu hỏi với hai đến bốn câu. Đưa ví dụ cá nhân, giải thích lợi ích của làm việc nhóm như hợp tác, giao tiếp và trách nhiệm chung, và nói tự nhiên trong suốt thời gian quy định.

body.prompt: Describe a time when you looked after a neighbour's pet. You should say: whose pet it was and what kind of animal it was; what you had to do to look after it; any problems or funny moments you experienced; and explain how you felt about the experience.

_provenance.cefr_reasoning: The task requires extended monologue narration with past-tense storytelling, describing experiences, problems, and reflections with some detail and cohesion. While the topic is everyday, the two-minute structured response with explanation of feelings and lessons learned demands B2-level discourse management, narrative complexity, and idiomatic expression beyond simple B1 description.

explanation.text: Introduce the pet and its owner, describe your daily responsibilities (feeding, walking, cleaning), mention one or two specific incidents, and finish with your feelings and what you learned from the experience.
explanation.text_vi: Giới thiệu con vật và chủ của nó, mô tả trách nhiệm hàng ngày (cho ăn, dắt đi dạo, dọn dẹp), kể một hoặc hai sự việc cụ thể, và kết thúc bằng cảm xúc của bạn cùng những gì bạn học được từ trải nghiệm này.

body.prompt: Describe a time when you volunteered or helped out at an organisation, such as an animal shelter. You should say: what the organisation was and what it did; what tasks you carried out there; who you worked with or met during the experience; and explain how this experience affected you or changed your views.

_provenance.cefr_reasoning: The task requires a two-minute structured monologue on a personal experience, combining concrete narration (past tenses, describing duties) with abstract reflection (how the experience changed views). This mix of concrete and abstract content, sustained discourse, and descriptive vocabulary aligns with B2 speaking descriptors.

explanation.text: Structure the response in four parts: introduce the organisation (an animal shelter), describe concrete duties such as feeding, walking dogs and cleaning kennels, mention the people involved (staff, other volunteers, adopters), and finish with personal reflection, e.g. increased empathy, responsibility or a decision to adopt rather than buy pets. Use past tenses and descriptive vocabulary to fill the full two minutes.
explanation.text_vi: Trình bày theo bốn phần: giới thiệu tổ chức (trạm cứu hộ động vật), mô tả công việc cụ thể như cho ăn, dắt chó đi dạo và dọn chuồng, nhắc đến những người gặp được (nhân viên, tình nguyện viên khác, người nhận nuôi), và kết thúc bằng suy nghĩ cá nhân, ví dụ sự đồng cảm tăng lên, tinh thần trách nhiệm hay quyết định nhận nuôi thay vì mua thú cưng. Dùng thì quá khứ và từ vựng miêu tả để nói đủ hai phút.

body.prompt: Describe how you or someone you know learned to read. You should say: when and how the learning began; who helped and what methods they used; what made reading easier or more difficult; and explain how learning to read has affected your life or that of the person you described.

_provenance.cefr_reasoning: This is a two-minute extended monologue with four structured cues, requiring sustained discourse, narrative past tenses, time expressions, and a reflective explanation of impact. The personal topic is accessible, but the demand for organized, extended speech covering abstract reflection (how learning to read affected one's life) and coherent multi-point development aligns with B2 speaking descriptors rather than B1's shorter, simpler exchanges.

explanation.text: Use the one-minute preparation to note ideas for each cue. Speak for the full two minutes, covering all four points in order, using past tenses and time expressions naturally, and finish with a reflective explanation of the impact of reading.
explanation.text_vi: Dùng một phút chuẩn bị để ghi ý cho từng gợi ý. Nói đủ hai phút, trình bày cả bốn điểm theo thứ tự, sử dụng thì quá khứ và cụm từ chỉ thời gian tự nhiên, và kết thúc bằng phần giải thích tác động của việc biết đọc.

body.prompt: Describe a time when you bought something second-hand, such as a used car or another pre-owned item. You should say: what you bought and why you decided to buy it second-hand; how you found it and what condition it was in; what problems or surprises you experienced; and explain whether you would buy second-hand again in the future.

_provenance.cefr_reasoning: The task requires an extended 2-minute monologue with structured narration in past tenses, evaluative opinion, and speculative future forms ('I might', 'I'd probably'). It demands organizing concrete and abstract content (reasons, problems, future intentions) with some idiomatic phrasing, matching B2 speaking descriptors rather than the simpler connected discourse of B1.

explanation.text: Structure your talk in four parts: introduce the item and your reasons for choosing second-hand, describe how you found it and its condition, mention any problems or unexpected issues, and finish with a clear opinion about buying second-hand in future. Use past tenses for the narrative and speculative language ('I might', 'I'd probably') for the future part.
explanation.text_vi: Trình bày bài nói theo bốn phần: giới thiệu món đồ và lý do chọn mua đồ cũ, mô tả cách bạn tìm được món đồ và tình trạng của nó, kể các vấn đề hoặc điều bất ngờ gặp phải, và kết thúc bằng ý kiến rõ ràng về việc có mua đồ cũ lần nữa hay không. Dùng thì quá khứ để kể chuyện và ngôn ngữ suy đoán ('I might', 'I'd probably') cho phần tương lai.

body.prompt: Describe a time when noise in a city affected you. You should say: where you were and what the noise was; how the noise affected you; what you did about it; and explain how you think cities could reduce noise pollution.

_provenance.cefr_reasoning: The task requires narrating a personal experience (past narration), describing effects on sleep, concentration and mood, and explaining abstract policy suggestions for reducing urban noise pollution. This combines concrete and abstract content, extended 2-minute discourse, and topic-specific vocabulary (noise pollution, traffic restrictions, construction regulations), matching B2 speaking descriptors.

explanation.text: Structure your talk in two minutes: set the scene (where and when), describe the noise and its effects on you (sleep, concentration, mood), explain how you responded, and finish with one or two realistic suggestions for reducing urban noise, such as traffic restrictions, better road surfaces, or stricter construction regulations.
explanation.text_vi: Sắp xếp bài nói trong hai phút: giới thiệu bối cảnh (ở đâu, khi nào), mô tả tiếng ồn và ảnh hưởng của nó (giấc ngủ, sự tập trung, tâm trạng), nói cách bạn đã xử lý, và kết thúc bằng một hoặc hai giải pháp thực tế để giảm tiếng ồn đô thị, như hạn chế giao thông, cải thiện mặt đường hoặc siết chặt quy định về xây dựng.

body.prompt: Describe a time when you grew vegetables or plants on a balcony or in a small space. You should say: what you grew and why you chose it; how you set up and looked after your little garden; what problems you faced and how you dealt with them; and explain whether growing your own food changed the way you think about eating or shopping.

_provenance.cefr_reasoning: The task requires a structured 2-minute monologue combining narrative past tenses with present-tense reflection, explaining problems and solutions, and discussing abstract effects on habits—matching B2 speaking descriptors (clear detailed description, explaining viewpoints with reasons).

explanation.text: Structure the talk in four parts: introduce what you grew and your reason, describe the setup and daily care routine, mention a specific difficulty such as lack of sunlight or pests and your solution, and finish with a reflection on how it affected your habits. Use past tenses for the story and present tenses for lasting effects.
explanation.text_vi: Trình bày bài nói theo bốn phần: giới thiệu loại rau bạn trồng và lý do, mô tả cách chuẩn bị và chăm sóc hàng ngày, nêu một khó khăn cụ thể như thiếu nắng hoặc sâu bệnh và cách giải quyết, kết thúc bằng suy nghĩ về việc nó ảnh hưởng đến thói quen ăn uống hay mua sắm của bạn. Dùng thì quá khứ để kể chuyện và thì hiện tại cho những ảnh hưởng lâu dài.

body.prompt: Now let's discuss large engineering projects and global trade. Consider these questions: 1) Why do you think nations have historically invested enormous resources in projects like the Suez Canal? 2) Some people argue that massive engineering projects bring more problems than benefits to local communities. What is your view? 3) How might international trade routes and shipping change in the next fifty years? 4) Do you believe countries should cooperate more on infrastructure that benefits everyone, such as canals and ports? Why or why not?

_provenance.cefr_reasoning: The task requires discussing abstract topics (global trade, infrastructure investment), evaluating arguments on both sides, and using speculative language about the future. Vocabulary like 'engineering projects,' 'trade routes,' and 'infrastructure' plus the need for sustained argumentation and hypothetical reasoning align with B2 descriptors for complex abstract discussion.

explanation.text: Develop each abstract question with a clear opinion, supporting reasons and examples. Use the Suez Canal as a reference point where relevant, discuss both sides briefly where asked, and use speculative language for future questions.
explanation.text_vi: Phát triển từng câu hỏi trừu tượng với quan điểm rõ ràng, lý lẽ và ví dụ hỗ trợ. Dùng kênh đào Suez làm ví dụ khi phù hợp, bàn luận cả hai mặt khi được yêu cầu, và dùng ngôn ngữ suy đoán cho các câu hỏi về tương lai.

body.prompt: Discussion questions: 1) Why do you think some people prefer buying a second-hand car rather than a brand-new one? 2) What are the possible risks of buying a used car, and how can buyers protect themselves? 3) Do you think second-hand markets for goods like cars, phones and furniture will grow in the future? Why or why not?

_provenance.cefr_reasoning: The task requires extended discourse on concrete and abstract topics (consumer behavior, market trends), speculative language, comparative structures, and discourse markers — all B2 speaking descriptors. The vocabulary (cost-effective, misled, second-hand markets) and the demand for reasoned argumentation with examples exceed B1 but do not require C1-level nuance.

explanation.text: Develop each answer with a clear opinion, supporting reasons and a brief example. Use comparative and speculative language (e.g. 'more cost-effective', 'buyers might be misled', 'this trend is likely to continue') and connect ideas with discourse markers such as 'on the other hand' and 'for instance'.
explanation.text_vi: Phát triển mỗi câu trả lời với quan điểm rõ ràng, lý do hỗ trợ và một ví dụ ngắn. Dùng ngôn ngữ so sánh và suy đoán (ví dụ 'more cost-effective', 'buyers might be misled', 'this trend is likely to continue') và liên kết ý tưởng bằng các từ nối như 'on the other hand' và 'for instance'.

body.prompt: IELTS Speaking Part 3 – Discussion. Answer the following questions in a natural, extended discussion. 1) Why do you think rivers change their course over time, and what effects can this have on the people who live nearby? 2) Some people believe humans should try to control rivers completely, while others argue we should adapt to natural changes. body.prompt: A local gym has announced that it is increasing its membership fees by 30% in order to fund new equipment and extended opening hours. body.model_answer:
In recent years, fitness has become an increasingly important part of many people's daily routines, and gyms play a central role in helping individuals stay healthy. When a gym raises its membership fees significantly, as in the case described, it inevitably provokes mixed reactions. While I accept that higher fees can fund genuine improvements, I believe that such steep increases risk excluding the very people who need exercise most.

On the one hand, there are clear arguments in favour of the price rise. Modern equipment and longer opening hours directly benefit members, making workouts more convenient and enjoyable. Furthermore, a well-maintained facility is safer and more motivating, which may attract new customers and ultimately stabilise the business. If a gym cannot invest in itself, its services may deteriorate and members may leave anyway.

On the other hand, a 30% increase is substantial, particularly for students, pensioners and low-income workers. For many, fitness is already a luxury rather than a necessity, and higher fees could force them to abandon exercise entirely, with negative consequences for public health. Moreover, there is no guarantee that the additional revenue will be spent wisely; members may feel they are paying more for the same service.

In my opinion, the gym should adopt a more balanced approach, such as introducing the increase gradually, offering discounted rates for students and off-peak users, or consulting members before making the decision. This would protect both the business and its community.

In conclusion, although investment in facilities is understandable, I believe a sharp fee increase is counterproductive, and a phased, inclusive pricing strategy would serve everyone better.

This matches B2 descriptors: complex text on abstract topics, structured argumentation, and technical/academic discussion.

explanation.explanation_en: A high-scoring IELTS Task 2 response addresses both views in the prompt, states a clear personal opinion, supports each point with developed reasons and examples, and organises ideas into clear paragraphs with an introduction and conclusion. Aim for at least 250 words with accurate complex grammar and a range of vocabulary.

Cần viết ít nhất 250 từ với ngữ pháp phức hợp chính xác và vốn từ phong phú.

body.model_answer: The discovery of penicillin by Alexander Fleming in 1928 is frequently cited as a fortunate accident: mould spores drifted into his laboratory and contaminated a bacterial culture, revealing a substance that could kill harmful bacteria. While chance clearly played a role, I would argue that such breakthroughs depend far more on preparation and a curious, observant mind than on luck alone. Admittedly, luck can open doors that no amount of planning could predict. Fleming did not set out to discover an antibiotic; the contamination was entirely unplanned, and a less tidy researcher might simply have discarded the dish. Similarly, many other advances, such as the discovery of X-rays, arose from unexpected observations. It would therefore be naive to deny that randomness contributes to scientific progress. However, chance only benefits those who are ready to recognise its significance. Fleming had spent years studying bacteria, so when he noticed the clear ring around the mould, he immediately understood what he was seeing and investigated further. Moreover, the discovery alone was not enough: over a decade later, Florey and Chain painstakingly developed penicillin into a usable drug, a triumph of systematic research rather than fortune. Had they lacked expertise and persistence, the mould on Fleming's dish would have remained a curiosity. In my view, the lesson of penicillin is that luck favours the prepared mind. Breakthroughs occur at the intersection of accident and readiness; without deep knowledge and disciplined work, even the most promising accident passes unnoticed. Governments and universities should therefore invest in training curious, well-prepared scientists, since they are the ones who can transform lucky moments into medical revolutions. In conclusion, while chance events like the contamination of Fleming's culture matter, preparation and perseverance are the decisive factors behind scientific discovery.

body.prompt: A well-known airline has announced that it will reduce the free checked baggage allowance from two pieces to one and charge extra fees for any additional bags. Some passengers see this as a fair way to keep ticket prices low, while others consider it an unfair extra cost. Write an essay for a university lecturer discussing both views and giving your own opinion. Write at least 250 words.

_provenance.cefr_reasoning: The task requires a discursive essay discussing two contrasting views with reasons, examples, and a personal opinion in at least 250 words for an academic audience. This matches IELTS Task 2-style demands typical of B2: argumentation, cohesive paragraphing, and a range of vocabulary and grammar on a concrete topic (travel/transport). It is beyond B1's simple connected text but does not require the nuanced, implicit, or highly advanced language of C1/C2.

explanation.explanation_en: A high-scoring response introduces the issue, discusses both views with supporting reasons and examples, states a clear personal opinion, and concludes logically. Aim for at least 250 words with well-linked paragraphs and a range of vocabulary and grammar structures.
explanation.explanation_vi: Một bài viết điểm cao cần giới thiệu vấn đề, thảo luận cả hai quan điểm kèm lý lẽ và ví dụ, nêu rõ ý kiến cá nhân và kết luận hợp lý. Viết ít nhất 250 từ với các đoạn văn liên kết chặt chẽ và vốn từ vựng, ngữ pháp phong phú.

body.model_answer:
In recent years, many airlines have revised their baggage policies in an effort to cut operating costs, and the decision by one major carrier to reduce the free checked allowance from two pieces to one has sparked considerable debate. While some travellers accept this change as a reasonable trade-off for cheaper fares, others view it as a hidden charge that penalises ordinary passengers. This essay will examine both perspectives before presenting my own view.

Supporters of the new policy argue that baggage handling is expensive, and that passengers who bring less luggage should not subsidise those who bring more. By charging separately for extra bags, airlines can advertise lower base fares, which benefits budget-conscious travellers who travel light. Furthermore, stricter limits may encourage people to pack more efficiently, which can speed up boarding and reduce delays at the gate.

On the other hand, critics contend that the change is essentially a price increase in disguise. Families, in particular, are likely to suffer, since a single checked bag is rarely enough for parents travelling with children. In addition, the fees for additional bags are often disproportionately high compared with the actual cost of carrying luggage, which suggests that the policy is designed to generate profit rather than to save money. Many passengers also feel misled, as the advertised fare no longer reflects the true price of the journey.

In my opinion, although the airline's argument has some economic logic, the policy places an unfair burden on those who genuinely need to carry more belongings. A fairer approach would be to offer modest discounts for light travellers while keeping a reasonable free allowance for everyone.

In conclusion, while reduced baggage allowances may lower headline prices, they risk alienating loyal customers. Airlines should balance cost savings with transparency and fairness if they wish to maintain passenger trust.

body.prompt: The invention of the telephone in the nineteenth century transformed the way people communicate. Some people believe that modern communication technologies, such as smartphones and the internet, have made face-to-face interaction less important. To what extent do you agree or disagree with this view? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

_provenance.cefr_reasoning: This is a classic IELTS Task 2 opinion essay requiring argumentation on an abstract topic (technology and communication), a formal academic register, 250+ words, varied linking devices, and structured paragraph development. These demands align with B2 descriptors: producing complex text on concrete and abstract topics with clear argumentation. The prompt itself is accessible, but the task requirements (position, justification, examples, formal register) exceed B1 and do not require C1-level nuance.

explanation.explanation_en: A high-scoring IELTS Task 2 response states a clear position in the introduction, develops two or three well-supported body paragraphs with examples, and reaches a conclusion that restates the position. Aim for at least 250 words, use a range of linking devices, and maintain a formal academic register throughout.
explanation.explanation_vi: Một bài viết IELTS Task 2 điểm cao cần nêu quan điểm rõ ràng trong phần mở bài, phát triển hai đến ba đoạn thân bài có lý lẽ và ví dụ cụ thể, và kết luận khẳng định lại quan điểm. Viết ít nhất 250 từ, sử dụng đa dạng từ nối và giữ văn phong trang trọng, học thuật.

body.model_answer: Since Alexander Graham Bell patented the telephone in 1876, communication technology has advanced at a remarkable pace. Today, smartphones and the internet allow people to contact one another instantly, wherever they are in the world. While some argue that these innovations have made face-to-face interaction less important, I largely disagree with this view. Admittedly, modern technology has reduced the need for certain types of in-person contact. Tasks that once required a meeting, such as arranging appointments or conducting routine business, can now be handled with a quick call or message. This undoubtedly saves time and money, particularly for companies with international clients. However, I would argue that digital communication complements rather than replaces personal interaction. Human relationships depend on trust, empathy and shared experience, none of which can be fully conveyed through a screen. For example, job interviews, medical consultations and family celebrations continue to take place face to face precisely because physical presence communicates nuances that text or voice cannot. Furthermore, rather than weakening personal bonds, technology often strengthens them. Video calls enable grandparents abroad to watch their grandchildren grow up, and messaging apps help friends maintain friendships across continents. In many cases, online contact actually leads to more frequent in-person meetings, as it makes arranging them easier. In conclusion, although the telephone and its modern descendants have changed how we communicate, they have not made face-to-face interaction less important. Instead, they have created new opportunities for connection, while the deepest and most meaningful communication still tends to happen in person.

body.topic: Work & Careers - hiring and training new staff at a small firm
body.prompt: Some people believe that small firms should invest more in training their existing staff rather than spending money on hiring new employees. Others argue that recruiting fresh talent is essential for a company's growth. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

_provenance.cefr_reasoning: This is a classic IELTS Task 2 discuss-both-views prompt requiring argumentation on an abstract work/careers topic, structured multi-paragraph essays, opinion statements, and topic-specific vocabulary (recruiting, training, staff retention). These demands align with B2: complex text on concrete and abstract topics with clear argumentation and linking. It does not require the nuanced, implicit, or highly sophisticated expression characteristic of C1/C2.

explanation.explanation_en: A high-scoring IELTS Task 2 response addresses both views in separate body paragraphs, states a clear personal opinion in the introduction and conclusion, and supports each point with relevant examples. Aim for at least 250 words with well-linked paragraphs and a range of vocabulary related to employment and business.

Cần viết ít nhất 250 từ với các đoạn văn liên kết chặt chẽ và vốn từ phong phú về việc làm và kinh doanh.

body.model_answer:
In today's competitive business environment, small firms often face difficult decisions about how to allocate limited resources. While some argue that developing current employees is the wiser investment, others believe that recruiting new talent is essential for growth. This essay will examine both perspectives before presenting my own view.

On the one hand, investing in existing staff has clear advantages. Employees who receive regular training tend to feel more valued, which increases motivation and reduces staff turnover. This is particularly important for small firms, where losing even one experienced worker can disrupt daily operations. Furthermore, training programmes allow companies to build specialised skills tailored to their specific needs, something that new hires may lack. For example, a small accounting firm that trains its assistants in the latest software can develop expertise that directly serves its clients.

On the other hand, hiring new employees brings fresh ideas and perspectives into the workplace. Newcomers often arrive with experience from other industries, which can stimulate innovation and challenge outdated practices. Recruitment also enables a firm to fill skill gaps quickly when the business expands into new areas, whereas training existing staff may take months or even years.

In my opinion, the best approach is a balanced one. Small firms should prioritise training their current workforce, as this builds loyalty and long-term capability, while remaining open to hiring when genuinely new skills are required. In conclusion, although recruitment has its benefits, I believe that developing existing employees offers greater value for small companies with limited budgets.

body.prompt: In many cities, car-sharing schemes have been introduced to help commuters travel more efficiently. Some people believe these schemes reduce traffic congestion and pollution, while others argue they are inconvenient and unreliable. To what extent do you agree or disagree that car-sharing schemes benefit commuters? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

_provenance.cefr_reasoning: The prompt requires an argumentative essay of at least 250 words with a clear position, counterargument acknowledgment, complex grammar, and varied linking devices. The topic (car-sharing, congestion, pollution) involves abstract discussion of societal issues, matching B2 descriptors for complex text on concrete and abstract topics. The 40-minute timed format and IELTS-style 'to what extent' task are typical of B2-level assessment.

explanation.explanation_en: A strong response states a clear position in the introduction, develops two or three well-supported arguments with examples, acknowledges the opposing view, and reaches a logical conclusion. Aim for at least 250 words with accurate complex grammar and a range of linking devices.

body.model_answer: In recent years, many urban authorities have launched car-sharing schemes in which commuters rent vehicles for short journeys instead of owning their own cars. While some critics question their practicality, I firmly believe that such schemes bring substantial benefits to both commuters and society as a whole. The most obvious advantage is environmental. When a single shared vehicle replaces several private cars, the total number of vehicles on the road falls, which eases congestion and lowers emissions. In my city, for example, a car-sharing pilot programme reportedly removed hundreds of private cars from the streets during rush hour, and average journey times improved noticeably. Secondly, car-sharing is often more economical for individuals. Owning a car involves considerable fixed costs, including insurance, parking and maintenance, whereas members of a sharing scheme pay only when they actually drive. For commuters who travel by public transport most days but occasionally need a car, this flexibility is ideal. Admittedly, opponents argue that shared cars may be unavailable at peak times or inconveniently located, and these concerns are legitimate. However, most modern schemes use mobile applications that allow users to locate and reserve vehicles in advance, which largely solves the reliability problem. Furthermore, as schemes expand, the density of available cars increases, making the service progressively more convenient. In conclusion, although car-sharing schemes are not perfect, their ability to reduce traffic, cut pollution and save commuters money makes them a valuable component of modern urban transport. Governments should therefore continue to invest in and promote them.
